newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Looser NZ budget seen sure bet post-election.
newsitem.headline: Looser NZ budget seen sure bet post-election.

text.p: New Zealand's first general election under proportional representaton is fraught with unknowns, but a sure bet is a looser fiscal stance, economists said on Friday.
"In our view, one of the safe bets to make about the post election environment is that fiscal policy will be loosened," said Bankers Trust NZ chief economist David Plank.
However, even worst case scenarios are far from bleak as New Zealand is one of the few countries in the world running budget surpluses and these are forecast to swell with no policy change.
"You are going to have to see something pretty drastic to see those surpluses completely wiped out," said Bain & Co economist Jill Patterson.

Treasury, in an assessment of the economy ahead of the October 12 election, forecast this year's surplus at NZ$2.9 billion, 3.1 percent of GDP. It saw this rising to $6.4 billion, 5.9 percent of GDP, in 1999/2000.

The Reserve Bank, in its September forecasts, was less optimistic, mainly because it projects a growth rate of 2.0 percent in the March 1997 year and 2.4 percent in 1998, against Treasury's 2.5 and 3.7 percent. It projects a surplus of $2.25 billion in 1996-97 and $1.89 billion the following year.
BTNZ estimates that even a government formed by the ruling conservative National Party government would raise spending by at least $750 million in 1997/98.
The new proportional system means coalition and minority governments are likely. Polls are indecisive, but suggest a left-of-centre government is more probable.
Private forecaster Infometrics, in a recent assessment of parties' fiscal policies, said all will produce surpluses, with left of centre Labour having the smallest at $1.66 billion in 1997/98.
It said all parties would increase spending, with the left-wing Alliance the biggest spender at $4.8 billion above current estimates for 1997/98.

However, the Alliance will, by raising taxes, produce the largest surplus in that year, at $3.7 billion.The economic nationalist New Zealand First party would increase spending by $1.7 billion to produce a surplus of $3.0 billion.

Bain & Co's Patterson said that from a financial markets perspective there were two main issues -- whether the fiscal "slippage" was inflationary, and what implications increased spending would have for the bond market programme.
On neither front does she predict strongly bearish outcomes.
"A lot of people say it would be a bit of a disaster, but we take the line it would depend very much how those spending initiatives are undertaken," she said of the fiscal slippage.

Plans by a left of centre government to spend more on health and education could be less inflationary than the second round of tax cuts announced by National for next year and already allowed for in monetary settings by the Reserve Bank, she said.
Under a Labour-led government with the more bearish Reserve Bank economic projections, bond issuance would be moderate at about $3 billion annually.

"Even under a Labour-led government we are still going to be looking at a contracting bond market (using RB fiscal projections) to the extent that the amount of bonds on issue will fall from $21 billion at June 1996 down to $16 billion by June 1999," she said.
Foreign investors are likely to welcome greater supply. Under the Treasury scenario with a National government, bonds on issue shrink from $21 billion to $12.4 billion by June 1999

"The fact that the bond market is contracting so significantly under a National-led government... that would be quite a worry, as some offshore investors might say they don't want to play the market because it is so small."
"A programme of between $3-4 billion is not by historical standards going to create a nightmare for the markets."

"You could run the argument that if supply is very limited then yields could go up. In some ways a bit of fiscal slippage as far as the bond market is concerned...from an offshore perspective, that probably isn't such a bad thing," she said.
